topic: Valve imports 13 tons of VR headsets
headline_marked: [[Valve imported 13 tons of VR headsets]] in a single day, likely for the Steam Frame
headline: Valve imported 13 tons of VR headsets in a single day, likely for the Steam Frame
summary: Valve's distribution partner offloaded nearly 32 metric tons of "Virtual Reality Devices" in Los Angeles, suggesting the first mass production shipment of the upcoming Steam Frame headset.
details: On June 10th, a German container ship docked in Los Angeles, offloading nearly 32 metric tons of "Virtual Reality Devices" for Valve. After subtracting container weight, this amounts to roughly 13 tons of actual product, likely the first mass production shipment of the Steam Frame headset.

This substantial import, noted by Valve watcher Brad Lynch, suggests fewer than 20,000 Steam Frame units, given each headset with controllers weighs about 654g. Valve has confirmed the Steam Frame will launch this summer.

In parallel, import records indicate Valve's stockpile of "Game Consoles," likely the Steam Machine, has grown to an estimated 141 metric tons since April 23rd. This could represent fewer than 50,000 units, considering each console weighs 2.6kg.

Valve previously announced both the Steam Machine and Steam Frame will launch this summer. The company also indicated it had to re-evaluate pricing due to component costs, but anticipates quick sell-outs despite potential higher prices.

topic: LLMs don't read, use weird trick instead
headline_marked: [[Your LLM can't read]]. Here's the weird trick it uses instead
headline: Your LLM can't read. Here's the weird trick it uses instead
summary: Large Language Models never actually "read" your words. Instead, they convert text into numerical tokens using a process called Byte Pair Encoding, which dictates how they process and are billed for input.
details: A core fact about Large Language Models is that they never truly "see" your words; they only process numbers. When you input text, it's first chopped into chunks called tokens, and each chunk is converted into an integer ID. The LLM then functions as a complex system mapping these integers to other integers.

Tokens are frequent text chunks, not always whole words or single letters. This process, known as Byte Pair Encoding, starts by combining the most common neighboring character pairs to build a vocabulary of 50k–100k chunks. Common words become single tokens, while rarer words are broken into multiple pieces.

This tokenization has significant practical implications, especially for billing and context window limits. Users are billed in tokens, not characters or words, and exceeding context windows is also measured by token count. Understanding tokenization is crucial for managing costs and preventing unexpected errors in production.

Many confusing behaviors observed in LLMs can be traced back to their tokenization process. Once you understand how text is broken down into tokens, seemingly strange model responses often become logical. This fundamental understanding is key to effectively working with and troubleshooting LLMs.
